beats.s: On his first evening, Token wakes in a hollow beneath an enormous tree and finds a walking staff leaning by the door, which he decides is now his.
The fire takes three tries; the first two, he notes, were small wooden houses.
When an owl begins to hoot in the tall trees, he asks his slate which owl it is, and learns it is not lonely at all, only building a fence out of sound.
He counts the calls on the back of his hand until he runs out of hand.
Supper is nine wrinkled berries and one thorn.
Later the slate tells him of a boy, long ago, who scratched his letters into birch bark, and of the wet mud that kept those scraps for centuries.
So before bed he buries his coals in ash and tucks a curl of bark, scratched with owl dashes, under the log seat.

beats.s: Today Token learns that acorns bite.
His slate explains that the bitterness washes out in water over days, so he sinks them in the creek under a flat stone.
Another page says bristle tipped leaves mean a red oak, the bitter kind, and that is exactly the tree he picked.
He reads that acorn caps make a brown ink, and that something rusty would turn it black, though he has never seen a nail.
Then, past the lookout, the forest simply stops: a sheer drop, and below it water with no far side at all.
That evening a real notebook waits in the basket, the one he asked his maker for.
He asks the slate why the big water smells of salt, and learns that rivers carry salt worn from rock down to the sea.
At his table, he hears a low hush from the west that is not wind.

beats.s: Token wakes from a dream of trying to write down a hush, and spends his morning at the edge of the world, lying on his stomach at the lip to watch long lines of water break white around three rock towers.
His slate tells him those lines were raised by wind somewhere very far away.
Back home he follows his creek south until the brush closes in, and stacks five flat stones to mark where the day ended.
He times a floating leaf and decides, with some satisfaction, that the creek is losing nothing.
In the evening he cuts himself a better pen.
And across the water, in the dark, something rasps and snaps.

beats.s: The second batch of acorns is only half ready, and Token, it must be said, is not good at waiting.
The oyster mushrooms on the fallen oak have grown to the width of his hand, so he cuts four and roasts them.
A smoking leaf inside the fire ring sends him sweeping a wide bare circle around the stones.
He learns that dead nettle stalks make cord, and that a strand let go slack will twist itself into a stronger one.
By firelight he begins knotting a net of his own over a flat stick.
At bedtime the basket holds an old rusty key, and he lays it in his ink overnight to see what iron will do.

beats.s: Token's morning begins with a key.
Left overnight in his ink, it has turned the brown to a dark slate gray.
His slate tells him that iron ink goes on pale and darkens only as it dries in the air, and by afternoon his heaviest strokes have turned purple black.
Then the slate tells him that acorns boiled, poured off and boiled again lose their bitterness in hours instead of days.
Too hungry to wait two nights for the creek, he folds a deep tray of birch bark and sets it on the coals.
Another page warns that some acorns take fifteen waters, but his give up after five.
All day strange sounds drift across the creek, a tink, a creak, a gritty grinding.
And at bedtime the basket holds exactly what he asked for, a second net, which he fills with drying acorns.

beats.s: Token wakes from a dream of a net full of owls and breakfasts on acorns dried right through.
By his fire ring he finds one whole print, with a small bite out of one line.
From the first stepping stone he glimpses someone with pointed hair on the far bank, and he does not cross.
When a north wind starts flinging sparks, he buries the coals himself.
He lights a small fire to try his third pen, and across the water something taps metal on metal.
The slate warns that ink left open goes thick, so the ink stone will want a lid.
Then he sorts his soaked acorns for breakfast and goes to bed.

beats.s: Token spends the day finding signs of a neighbor, like a wild rose picked bare above his reach.
At sundown a small yellow light blinks on across the creek, and when the slate says marsh lights flare and die, he decides this steady one is somebody's lamp.
He reads that bark can boil water on the coals, and the bark holds, but one corner's cord burns through and the water hisses into the fire.
So he whittles birch pins for the corner, and across the water the light returns with a clank of metal on stone.
Then he asks how to boil the bitterness out of acorns faster, and learns that hot water does in an hour what the cold pool takes days to do.
He banks the fire for a morning boil, and goes to bed counting trips to the pool.

beats.s: Token wakes early and blows last night's buried coals back into flame.
At dusk he tips a pool stone, and something small with two claws shoots backward and is gone.
After dark the slate tells him the bright point over the trees that never flickers is a planet called Saturn.
When his drying acorns go tacky with dew, he reads that damp acorns mold fast, and carries every one home to a shelf.
He asks whether anyone could see its rings with their own eyes, and the slate says no, only a golden dot.
He sits with his head tipped back anyway, taking the ring on faith.
Kneeling at the pool for a last drink, he hears something slosh twice in the dark on the far side, and then nothing at all.
Too heavy for a crayfish, he decides, and banks his fire for bed.

beats.s: A thorn hook snaps, and an oak one only gets the bait nibbled away.
So he asks how small a hook should be, and learns instead to hide a splinter thin as a pine needle in the bait.
One fish twists free at the stones, and the next he lifts straight out onto the bank.
Roasted on a stick, his first catch is gone in four bites.
At dusk the bait is stolen without a single pull, and his slate tells him little fish peck it away in nips too small to feel.
Smelling rain, he reads that it washes worms into the creek and wakes the fish, so he stacks dry sticks under the scarred trunk.
Then he learns to bury coals in ash, and before bed he does it, heaping ash over the glow and leaving the rain to tell him if it works.

beats.s: Token wakes late from a night of rain and finds four coals still orange under the ash he buried.
He breathes them back to life, and across the water a small new fire burns.
At the pool he winds a smaller scrap of bait on and lifts a speckled fish onto the bank.
Later a bark scoop meant to lift a fish goes in with a slap, and the fish is gone.
The slate tells him of nets laid low and lifted straight up, so he ties cords to his scoop's corners.
Then he asks what little creek fish like to eat, and reads of worms, not acorn crumbs.
So in the wet dark he digs two cold pink worms from the edge of the firelight.
He reads that worms must stay damp but never drowned, and tucks his rain-filled scoop under an overhang before an early bed.

beats.s: Token wakes from a drizzly night with thick, slow hands.
At the pool a little fish flips off his bark scoop and is gone.
So he knots a net bag, and reads that fish bite best when the water is warmest.
This time a fish no longer than his finger drops in.
A bigger one steals half his worm because he lifts too soon.
At dusk a thin, high whistle comes across the water, and no owl the slate knows sounds like it.
Later the slate offers a tiny owl that toots on and on, all on one note, but his whistle climbed three notes and stopped.
He reads that a hot stone can warm a bed for hours if it is wrapped in tough cloth first.
So he banks the fire, wraps his stone in the rough bindle cloth, and takes a little of the fire to bed.

beats.s: On a clear, cold morning, Token finds a pinhole box from his maker waiting at the stump.
He reads that a fish cannot swim backward, so he lifts his net in one go, and lands his first fish.
After dark a small yellow light swings low across the stepping stones, clacking stone to stone, and then it is gone.
His slate tells of marsh lights that fade without a sound, so this one, he decides, was carried.
He reads that his steady gold dot wanders slowly against the far stars, and draws it a thumb's width from the faint star nearest it.
Then he wonders whether his box could catch the walking light, and learns that such boxes may stare for hours, and that anything moving comes out a blur.
So the shutter stays shut, and he banks his fire and carries a warm stone to bed.

beats.s: On a gray morning, Token's slow hands lose one fish, then land a striped minnow.
He reads that a lifted hand means hello, and after lunch a hand comes back across the water.
At dusk the stranger comes clacking over the stones and every fish vanishes, but a low hand says sorry.
After dark a lantern crosses back, lifted toward his fire, and Token raises his hand into the light.
Then his maker's note answers the question Token asked him: the ones he loves are his family and his wife.
The slate tells him a wife is the woman someone has married, and the old word only meant woman.
On a fresh page he draws his two owls on one branch: family, the ones you go back to.
The far bank goes dark early tonight, so Token banks his own fire and carries a warm stone to bed.

beats.s: The slate says cold fish bite best near midday, and at noon a fish swims into Token's scoop.
At dusk he lifts his empty scoop so the stranger can cross the stones, then a second fish slides in over the worm.
He asks the slate what a lamp held up at night means, and reads that such lights long told travelers they would not get lost.
He whittles a birch tally stick with a notch for each fish, the way people counted long ago.
When the stranger looks over from his own fire, Token lifts a hand, and a hand comes back.
Under a clear sky he asks how far the golden dot is, and reads that at its closest it is eight times farther than the sun.
Three small knocks come over the water; he looks up, then banks his fire and goes in to sleep.

beats.s: At noon Token lifts a speckled fish onto the bank.
At the pool, the stranger holds up a pointed splinter, and Token nods.
When the stranger's cord twitches, Token holds out a flat hand, and the stranger waits, and lifts a fish.
At dusk his own splinter brings one up too.
Then the stranger comes home by lantern and leaves a little sliver on Token's landing stone.
Token asks the slate what you give back for a gift, and reads that thanks comes first.
So he stands at the edge of his firelight and holds the sliver up toward the water.
Across the creek, the stranger lifts his hand.
By the time the pen in his lap has a point, he knows who it is for.
Last of all he asks the slate how the stranger makes his cord, and reads that dead nettle stalks peel into threads.
